content: The ideal scenario for determining the size of a facility is to have a record of its dimensions in square meters or, even better, a map with detailed floor plans. If such records are unavailable, alternative methods for estimating the facility's size can be explored, such as those outlined in the building space section. The operating hours of the entire facility and the tuberculosis (TB) services (e.g., regular TB clinic hours) should be documented. This includes specifying the days of the week the facility is open and services are provided, as well as the total hours of operation for both the facility and TB services over a seven-day week. The total number of hospital beds (inpatient) should be reported for the entire hospital, as well as specifically for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB), multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), and TB-HIV patients. Similarly, the number of day beds (outpatient), which may also be referred to as cots or gurneys, should be reported for the same categories. Information about TB services offered at the facility should include treatment services, patient support during diagnosis or treatment, and community services provided through or to the facility. Additional service outputs relevant to the facility can be selected from dropdown menus in categories such as visit and bed-day types, laboratory tests, radiology tests, and other TB services. Examples of other TB services include lost-to-follow-up tracing via home visits, contact tracing, education or health talks, adherence support, or infection control. If additional service outputs are required but not listed, they can be added to the relevant category in the Lists sheet at the end of the tool by entering the name of the service output in the designated yellow cells. The value of the building can be determined by obtaining the current replacement value for a similar type of building in a comparable location (urban, peri-urban, or rural). This valuation can be sourced from architects, structural engineers, scientific research centers, or construction companies. Alternatively, original facility records from the time of construction, sourced from the administrative department or government records, can be adjusted for inflation to estimate the current value. If these options are unavailable, other methods such as insurance valuations, cost per square meter in the area, tax forms, or government stamp duty rates can be used. For recently renovated buildings, costs can be adjusted using the consumer price index (CPI) for the country. If the facility or parts of it are rented, the rental value can be found in the lease agreement or sourced from the finance department or leasing agency. If the total land area is known but not the building size, the proportion of land occupied by the building can be estimated and multiplied by the total land size and the number of floors (if it is a multi-story building). It is advisable to check for or create a map of the facility, noting shared spaces and how they are allocated (e.g., specific days or time divisions). For TB services provided in designated spaces, the total space used for TB can be calculated by summing the areas utilized for TB services in square meters. Shared spaces should be noted, and specific allocations for TB services should be calculated. Spaces no longer in use, such as abandoned or derelict areas, should not be included, but empty space should be accounted for. To avoid double counting, either the total square meter value for a department or its subsets should be recorded, but not both. Recurrent overhead costs for the entire facility, such as water, electricity, gas, bio-safety disposal, internet, telephone, and administrative expenses, should be documented. These costs are often sourced from facility expenditure records. Overhead inputs shared across departments (e.g., maintenance, transport, electricity) should be allocated to cost centers based on defined allocation methods, such as patient-day equivalents or floor space utilized by departments. It is important to distinguish between facility-level overhead costs and above-service-level costs to prevent double counting. Transportation data should include vehicles used for TB-related activities, such as transporting specimens, supplies, drugs, or patients, as well as staff providing TB services. Data should be sourced from the finance and human resources departments and include both facility-owned and courier services. The allocation of vehicle usage for TB should be estimated based on time or mileage dedicated to TB services. Training costs for TB-related staff training should be documented, including venue costs, catering, facilitator fees, and training materials. Training that benefits the facility directly is considered a facility-level cost, while training provided by external sources (e.g., National TB Program) is categorized as above-service-level cost. Training data should include the duration, number of staff trained, and associated costs. Equipment and furniture used for TB services should be inventoried, with details such as manufacturer, model, and percentage of use for TB services. Replacement costs should be used as the standard value for unit pricing. Equipment not used for TB services should not be included. Broken equipment that was used in the last year and is planned for repair or replacement should be costed, but derelict equipment that is no longer functional and not expected to be used again should not. Drug prices for TB treatment, prevention, and palliative care should be collected, including unit prices in local currency and USD. Supplies used for TB care should also be inventoried, with any additional items not listed added to the appropriate section. Data should be sourced from the facility or central sources such as the Ministry of Health or regional health authorities.
